These structures provide mechanistic insights into R2Tg-mediated TPRT in its natural context and in the programmable gene integration system STITCHR (site-specific target-primed insertion through targeted CRISPR homing of retroelements). Furthermore, we combine these structural insights with computational protein design methods to engineer an enhanced STITCHR system.

title: A nanoscale map of the human cell surface proteome reveals spatial and functional organization
abstract: The cell surface proteome governs processes essential for development, immunity and disease, yet its large-scale spatial organization remains uncharted. Here, we systematically map the surface proteome of human T lymphocytes and B lymphoblasts using proximity labeling of 85 antigens. Coupled with data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry, this approach reveals functional modules, including known complexes such as the T cell receptor alongside clusters not previously implicated in cell membrane functions. Notably, we identify mitochondrial proteins at the surface, suggesting that they may bear underappreciated roles at the plasma membrane. A machine learning classifier predicts surface protein associations, revealing the IL-10 receptor beta subunit’s regulation of type I interferon signaling. Spatial modeling distinguishes widely dispersed from localized antigens, indicating active mechanisms of surface organization. In summary, this work provides a large-scale map of the human surfaceome and a resource for exploring its spatial and functional organization.

title: Q&A with Bil Clemons
abstract: Bil Clemons is the Hanisch Memorial Professor of Biochemistry at Caltech, where he leads a research group applying structural biology approaches to study membrane protein biogenesis and peptidoglycan biosynthesis in bacteria. He is also a scientist-in-residence at the Biohub. Here, I asked Bil about his journey to becoming the scientist he is today, advances in structural biology, and the field of protein biogenesis and balancing great science with humanity.

title: EMC chaperone activity is required for cotranslational calcium channel assembly
abstract: Nearly half of the ~5,000 human membrane proteins need to assemble into stoichiometric complexes as part of their biogenesis at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane. How ER-resident biogenesis factors coordinate membrane insertion, folding and assembly is not well understood. Here we demonstrate that the human ER membrane protein complex (EMC) insertase additionally acts as a chaperone to facilitate the assembly of heterotrimeric voltage-gated calcium channels (Ca v ). Using function-separating mutations and inhibitory nanobodies, we show that nascent Ca v channels are degraded prematurely when EMC’s chaperone function is selectively perturbed. Blocking EMC’s chaperone function impaired Ca v -dependent cardiomyocyte contraction. EMC engagement of the pore-forming Ca v α-subunit occurred cotranslationally and required the Ca v α-subunit’s first transmembrane domain bundle to protrude from the nascent ribosome–multipass translocon complex. Our findings establish a chaperone function for the EMC and suggest that biogenesis of multibundle membrane proteins may require a highly orchestrated, cotranslational interplay among ER biogenesis factors.

title: Large-scale RNA-binding protein tethering screen discovers modulators of circular RNA metabolism
abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are emerging as important regulators in mammalian cells and promising substrates for RNA therapeutics, yet the trans -acting factors governing their metabolism remain poorly defined. Here we systematically evaluate 730 RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) using a tethered reporter assay and identify 281 RBPs that significantly modulate circRNA activity. Follow-up assays implicate these RBPs across key stages of the circRNA life cycle, including biogenesis, nuclear export, degradation and translation. We identify seven RBPs for tethered translation enhancement of therapeutically applicable circRNA vectors and highlight LARP4B as a potent enhancer of exogenous circRNA translation across multiple internal ribosomal entry sites and cell types. We uncover an evolutionarily conserved role for RBM15 in circRNA biogenesis in fly, mouse and human, further demonstrating a role in circRNA nuclear retention, and that perturbing RBM15 sites with dCasRx or antisense oligonucleotides modulates endogenous circRNA expression. Together, our study provides a global view of circRNA trans -regulation and describes practical entry points for therapeutic development.
